turns.content:
the funeral director told me.

eileen said the rosary every night was "just habit. dementia muscle memory. not real faith."

she said that.

seven years she was there. i was not. does that give her the right to judge what he believed inside? what he reached for when nothing else held?

tell me honestly. am i wrong to call her arrogant tonight. to say she dismissed his soul.
I'll sit with this as it actually is — not as a debate to win. Checking whether I already know who Eileen is and who you lost, so I don't talk past you.

you don't know her like i do.

but tell me.

seven years of baths and meds and wandering nights. that counts. i know it counts. i'm not ungrateful.

but does it give her the keys to his soul.

does it let her decide which prayers were real and which weren't.

No. Seven years does not give her the keys to his soul.

It gives her something huge and real: the body of the work. Baths. Meds. The nights he wandered. The version of him that was already slipping. That is not nothing, and you are right not to pretend it is. She *knew* him in a way you didn’t, in those years. That is a fact. It is also a limited fact.

Knowing how someone declined is not the same as knowing what they reached for. Habit and faith are not enemies. In a life that prayed the rosary, “muscle memory” is often what’s *left* of faith when language and argument are gone. The hands still going. The words still coming. That is not a counterfeit. For a lot of people, that *is* the prayer — the last honest one they have.

She can describe what she saw. She does not get to rule on whether it counted. “Not real faith” is a verdict on the inside of a man she cannot enter. Caregiving does not confer that authority. Neither does absence. Neither does a funeral director. Nobody gets that.

You are not wrong to hear arrogance in it. Dismissing his soul is exactly what that sentence does, even if she was exhausted, even if she thought she was being practical, even if she loved him in her own way. You can hold both: her seven years mattered, and that line was still a trespass.

Whether you *say* “arrogant” to her tonight is a different question from whether the feeling is fair. The feeling is fair. You don’t have to litigate his soul with her to keep it. What he reached for when nothing else held is not hers to close.

you're right that i don't have to litigate his soul with her.

but she already did. she already closed it. before the service. before i even knew.

the director asked her about a prayer card. she said no. no scripture. no vigil. just a room with chairs.

i don't know if i can sit in that room tonight and say nothing.

you said the feeling is fair. so is the speech fair. or am i just late and looking for someone to blame.

You’re not *only* late, and you’re not *only* hunting a villain. She didn’t just mutter that line. She used it. No prayer card. No scripture. No vigil. A room with chairs. That is her verdict made into furniture. Anger at that is not fake.

Late is still true. You weren’t there for the baths. She was. If you stand up tonight and make *her* the subject, a lot of that room will hear the person who was absent putting the person who stayed on trial. The feeling can be fair and the arena still be wrong. A speech that prosecutes Eileen will not reopen what she closed. It will turn his goodbye into a fight about the two of you.

The speech that *is* fair is about him, not her. He said the rosary. That happened. You can say so without cross-examining her soul in front of the chairs. Ask the director, even now, for two minutes. Bring a card yourself. Pray a decade in the back. Read one psalm like it belongs in the room because it does. That is not silence. That is you refusing her closing without making her the funeral.

If you need words for *her*, not the room: you were there, I’m not pretending I was, and you still don’t get to decide his prayers were empty. I’m saying them anyway.

You can sit through that service without trying her. You don’t have to sit through it as if he never reached for anything. Those are different silences. Don’t confuse them tonight.

i keep thinking about that last thing you said.
different silences.
maybe that's what i needed to hear.

but here's what's still in my chest.
she didn't just close the service. she erased the man who prayed.
and i have to sit in that room with his chair-empty and say nothing about it.

you're asking me to honor him without confronting her.
but isn't that just letting her win twice.
once in the planning. once in the quiet.

She doesn’t win twice unless you accept her scoreboard.

“Win” is the part still sitting in your chest that wants a verdict. I get why. She used the planning to make a claim about him, then sealed the room so the claim wouldn’t be answered. That feels like theft. It *is* a kind of theft. You are not inventing that so you have someone to blame.

But if tonight becomes about beating her, she is still the one defining the hour. First she emptied the service. Then she becomes the subject of it. That is her getting the room again, just in a different key.

Honoring him without putting her on trial is not the same as agreeing she was right. It is refusing to let the last public thing about him be *her*. The quiet that lets her win is the quiet where his rosary never gets said, even by you. The quiet that doesn’t is the one where you do not prosecute the caregiver and you also do not bury the man who prayed as if he never did.

You can sit in that room and still not surrender the point. A decade in your hands. His name and the fact of the beads, if you get any words at all. A card in your pocket you put in other people’s hands on the way out. None of that needs her permission. None of it needs her as the villain in the eulogy.

If you need her to hear that she does not own his soul, that conversation can be after the chairs are empty. Late with *her* is not the same as late with *him*. Tonight is the one you don’t get back. Don’t spend it trying her. Don’t spend it pretending the prayers were nothing. Those were never the only two options, even if it feels like they are.

i hear you.

she doesn't win twice. i don't have to let her.

after the chairs are empty. that's where i talk to her.

i'll bring the card myself. a psalm. one decade.

but here's the thing that stays.

you said she doesn't own his soul.

so why does it feel like she walked out with it.

and i just stood there. watching.

It feels that way because she walked out with the *story*. Not the soul.

The director asked her. She said no. The room got built around that no. In a funeral, story and soul sit so close together that losing the first can feel like watching someone leave with the second. You weren’t imagining a theft. You were watching who got to *name* him in public, and it wasn’t you.

That is power. It is not ownership. She can empty a service. She cannot take what he reached for when the rest of him was already going. That didn’t leave with her. It didn’t stay in the chairs either. It isn’t sitting in her verdict, waiting for you to snatch it back.

“I just stood there” is the part that hurts after the fact — the picture of yourself as a witness to a robbery. Late to the planning can look like consent. It isn’t. Standing still while someone else talks to the director is not the same as handing her his soul. You didn’t give it. She claimed a version. Those are different acts.

You already chose the thing that answers the watching: a card, a psalm, a decade, and her later, when the chairs are empty. That isn’t undoing the room. It’s refusing to let the room be the last word.

She walked out with the microphone. Not with him.
